topic: Translating business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
question_text: A financial services company wants to reduce the time analysts spend reading regulatory filings. They currently have analysts spend 3 hours summarizing each filing. Which approach best translates this business problem into a Claude-based solution?

options.text: Build a retrieval system that fetches relevant regulatory filings when analysts request them.
Use Claude to generate concise summaries of regulatory filings with key risk flags highlighted, replacing the manual reading step.
Create a database of past analyst summaries and use Claude to search through them.
Deploy Claude as a chatbot that answers analyst questions about regulatory topics in general.

explanation: The business problem is reducing the time cost of summarizing filings — option B directly addresses this by automating the summarization step with Claude. Options A and D shift the task rather than automating the existing workflow. Option C leverages past summaries but still requires analysts to read those summaries and does not handle new filings automatically.

question_text: A healthcare provider wants to build a patient triage assistant that collects symptoms, asks clarifying questions, and routes patients to the right care level. Which end-to-end architecture best represents this solution?

options.text: User input → Claude summarization → database storage → manual review by staff.
User input → Claude conversational agent (symptom collection + multi-turn Q&A) → structured triage output → routing logic → care level assignment with human-in-the-loop escalation.
User input → keyword extraction → hard-coded rule engine → care level assignment.
User input → fine-tuned small model classification → care level assignment without human review.

explanation: A triage assistant requires multi-turn conversation to gather symptoms progressively, structured output for routing, and human-in-the-loop escalation for safety-critical decisions. Option B captures all these stages. Options C and D bypass conversational intelligence, and option A lacks both routing logic and human oversight.

topic: Translating business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
question_text: A legal firm wants to speed up contract review. Associates currently read contracts and flag clauses that deviate from standard terms. What is the most direct translation of this business problem into a Claude workflow?

options.text: Provide Claude with the contract and a set of standard terms; instruct it to identify and explain deviating clauses.
Use Claude to rewrite contracts to match standard terms automatically.
Build a chatbot where associates can ask Claude general legal questions.
Train a classification model on past contracts to predict clause risk scores.

explanation: The core task is clause deviation detection — option A replicates the associate's workflow by giving Claude the contract alongside standard terms and asking for differences. Option B changes the output from flagging to rewriting, which exceeds the stated requirement. Options C and D are less direct translations of the specific clause-review task.

question_text: A company deploys a Claude-based customer support agent. After launch, the team wants to continuously improve answer quality. Which architecture element is most important to add for enabling systematic improvement?

options.text: Increase the context window size to handle longer customer queries.
Add a feedback loop that captures user ratings and agent-flagged low-confidence responses, feeding them back into evaluation and prompt iteration cycles.
Switch to a larger Claude model for all requests.
Add more example conversations to the system prompt.

explanation: Continuous improvement requires a structured feedback loop: capturing signals (ratings, low-confidence flags), analyzing them, and iterating on prompts or configurations. This closes the improvement cycle in the architecture. Options A, C, and D are point-in-time optimizations that do not create a self-improving system.

question_text: A retail company wants to build a product recommendation assistant that accesses customer purchase history and current inventory. What are the critical architectural components? (Select TWO)

options.text: A retrieval layer that fetches customer purchase history and live inventory data at query time.
A fine-tuned model trained exclusively on the company's product catalog.
A system prompt that defines the assistant's persona and constrains recommendations to in-stock items.
A separate Claude instance for each product category.

explanation: A recommendation assistant needs dynamic data access (option A — retrieval layer for purchase history and inventory) and behavioral constraints (option C — system prompt limiting to in-stock items and defining the assistant's role). Fine-tuning on a static catalog (B) would quickly go stale as inventory changes, and per-category instances (D) create unnecessary complexity and cost.

topic: Translating business requirements to architecture decisions
question_text: A manufacturing company wants to reduce equipment downtime by detecting anomalies in sensor logs and suggesting maintenance actions. The solution must explain its reasoning to maintenance engineers. Which combination of architectural elements is essential?

options.text: A tool that reads sensor log files or a time-series database to supply context to Claude.
A black-box anomaly detection model that outputs a binary alert with no explanation.
Claude generating a natural-language explanation of the detected pattern and suggested maintenance action.
A fully automated system that triggers maintenance without engineer review.

explanation: The solution needs access to sensor data (option A — tool or retrieval layer) and explainable output in natural language (option C — Claude's explanation capability). A black-box model (B) cannot satisfy the requirement for reasoning transparency. Fully automated maintenance without engineer review (D) contradicts the requirement to communicate with engineers and creates safety risks in a manufacturing context.

question_text: A downstream billing service consumes Claude's output and requires a strict JSON schema. In the end-to-end design, enforcing that output contract should be owned by:

options.text: The input-handling stage, by rejecting requests that lack schema hints
The output-delivery stage, validating schema before returning results
The feedback loop, by flagging malformed responses after delivery
The processing stage, trusting the model to always emit valid JSON

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1B1 Design end-to-end architectures | Key Concept: output-delivery stage. The output stage owns shaping and validating results for the consumer. A strict schema for a downstream service is a programmatic guardrail enforced in code at delivery, not a hope that the model complies, so malformed payloads never leave the system.

question_text: A cohesive summarization task fits comfortably in one context window and reads as a single coherent request. An engineer proposes splitting it into five subagents to seem more robust. Latency and simplicity matter. Which approach is best?

options.text: Split into five subagents, since decomposition always improves reliability on essentially any task.
Handle it in one well-structured prompt, since the task is cohesive and fits in context.
Use an orchestrator-worker design to add the isolation this summarization inherently requires.
Chain five sequential calls so each subagent refines the previous step's summary.

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1B2 Select architectural patterns | Key Concept: decomposition versus monolithic prompt. Decomposition improves reliability on genuinely multi-part tasks but adds handoff overhead and failure points; a cohesive task that fits in context is better served by one well-structured prompt. Do not decompose reflexively.

topic: pattern selection favors the least complex option
question_text: A team must add a single fixed processing step to summarize incoming tickets, with control flow fully owned by developers. Which pattern BEST fits this bounded requirement?

options.text: A multi-agent orchestrator delegating summaries to specialized worker subagents
An augmented LLM call with retrieval and developer-defined control flow
An autonomous agent that dynamically decides each processing step itself
A routing workflow classifying tickets across several specialized model paths

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1A1 Business-to-Solution Translation | Key Concept: pattern selection favors the least complex option. A single fixed step with developer-owned control flow is served by an augmented LLM, the lowest-complexity building block. Added autonomy must be justified by a requirement a simpler pattern cannot meet.

task_statement: 1C2 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
question_text: A summarization service condenses a single cohesive document into one paragraph. The task fits comfortably within context, has no separable parts, and latency is the binding SLA for the service. A team proposes a five-step chain plus a reviewer subagent to appear rigorous. Reliability is already acceptable with a single prompt. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Adopt the five-step chain, since more steps always raise output quality
Add the reviewer subagent to catch any rare summarization error later
Split the document into sections handled by separate parallel subagents
Keep the single prompt; the cohesive task meets the latency SLA

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1C2 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving | Key Concept: resist reflexive decomposition. A cohesive task that fits in context and already meets reliability is best served by one prompt. When latency is the binding SLA, added chains and subagents impose coordination cost and threaten the SLA for no benefit.

question_text: A team insists their system is 'agentic' because it calls tools and retrieves documents. In their design, the developer's code fixes the exact sequence of tool calls every run. How should the pattern be classified?

options.text: An augmented LLM, since a fixed developer control flow is not agentic
An agent, because using tools and retrieval alone makes a system agentic
A multi-agent system, since each tool acts as an autonomous subagent
An agent-to-agent design, given the coordination across multiple tool calls

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1B2 Select appropriate architectural patterns | Key Concept: distinguishing augmented from agentic. A system where developer code fixes the exact step sequence is an augmented LLM, not an agent, no matter how many tools it invokes. The line is dynamic, model-directed control flow; without it, tool use alone is not agentic.

task_statement: 1A2 Align solutions to business value pillars
topic: balance competing pillars instead of discarding one
question_text: A fraud-review copilot must cut analyst review time (productivity), stay under a per-case cost cap (cost), and respond within two seconds (performance SLA). Load tests show the largest model meets accuracy and latency but blows the cost cap at production volume, roughly tripling the projected monthly spend. Which approach BEST balances all three stated pillars?

options.text: Standardize on the largest model and renegotiate the per-case cost cap upward
Batch all cases overnight to capture the roughly-half asynchronous pricing discount
Drop the two-second latency target so the largest model fits the budget
Route routine cases to a smaller model, escalating only hard ones upward

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1A2 Align solutions to business value pillars | Key Concept: balance competing pillars instead of discarding one. Routing routine cases to a smaller model and escalating only hard cases keeps most traffic cheap and fast while spending capability where it pays off, honoring cost, latency, and accuracy at once. Renegotiating the cap, batching a real-time flow, or dropping the SLA each solve one pillar by abandoning another.

task_statement: 1C1 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
question_text: In a multi-agent design, an orchestrator delegates a subtask to a subagent. Regarding the subagent's context, which statement is correct?

options.text: Context must be explicitly passed in the handoff; it is not inherited
The subagent automatically inherits the orchestrator's full conversation context
Sharing all orchestrator context with every subagent is always safest
Subagents share a single context pool the framework maintains automatically

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1C1 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies | Key Concept: unshared context as the default. In multi-agent orchestration, subagents do not inherit the orchestrator's context; it must be explicitly passed in the handoff. Forgetting this is a primary cause of multi-agent failures, and broad sharing to compensate raises cost and leakage risk.

task_statement: 1C1 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
question_text: A bank wants an AI system that files regulatory reports. The steps are known and fixed, every filing is high-stakes and legally consequential, and errors must be caught before submission. A team proposes an autonomous multi-agent design for flexibility. As the architect weighing patterns, governance, and risk, what do you recommend?

options.text: An autonomous multi-agent system, because agentic flexibility handles regulatory edge cases best
A predictable workflow with programmatic guardrails and human review before each filing
Multiple negotiating agents so they cross-check each other and entirely skip human review
A single prompt with a prompt-based instruction telling it not to make mistakes

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1C1 Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies | Key Concept: pattern plus governance. Known, fixed steps favor a predictable, auditable workflow over autonomy. Legally consequential, irreversible actions require programmatic guardrails and human-in-the-loop review before submission, because guardrails reduce but do not bound risk. The best design pairs the least complex pattern with high-stakes gating.

task_statement: 1A2 Align solutions to business value pillars
topic: measure the pillar you are claiming
question_text: An internal drafting assistant is proposed to raise analyst output on routine client memos. Sponsors want a single headline number to track its business value across the whole team over each quarter. Which metric BEST expresses the productivity pillar for this particular use case?

options.text: Total monthly API spend aggregated across all participating analysts
Drafts per analyst hour, compared before and after adoption
Average model response latency measured across all drafting requests
Number of model calls issued during a typical drafting session

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1A2 Align solutions to business value pillars | Key Concept: measure the pillar you are claiming. A productivity claim is verified by output per unit of human effort, so drafts completed per analyst hour against a baseline is the fitting metric. Spend, latency, and raw call counts measure other pillars or mere activity, and none of them shows that analysts actually produce more.

task_statement: 1A1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
topic: at scale, progressive discovery beats monolithic context
question_text: An agent integration must scale to a large, growing set of tools across many services. Loading every tool definition upfront has caused rising cost, latency, and increasingly confused tool selection. The team wants a structural pattern here, not incremental prompt tuning or description edits. Which of the following BEST describes the right approach?

options.text: Monolithic context loading, since front-loading every definition is most reliable at scale
A single larger model whose wider context window absorbs all the tool definitions
Splitting the tools evenly across several parallel agents that share full context
Progressive discovery, letting the agent find and load only the tools it currently needs

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1A1 Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions | Key Concept: at scale, progressive discovery beats monolithic context. Loading tool definitions on demand as the task requires keeps a large, growing toolset tractable and counters the capability bloat, cost, and latency that front-loading every definition causes.

topic: production monitoring in the feedback loop
question_text: A summarization service passed all pre-deployment evals and shipped. Two months later users report drift in quality, but the team has no signal until complaints arrive. They pass offline evals whenever they re-run them. Which gap in the end-to-end design explains this, and what closes it?

options.text: Missing production monitoring; add live metrics to the loop
Weak offline evals; expand the held-out test set substantially
Model too small; upgrade to a more capable model tier
Insufficient logging; increase log verbosity across all requests

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1B1 Design end-to-end architectures | Key Concept: production monitoring in the feedback loop. Pre-deployment evals do not catch live drift. A complete end-to-end design instruments production with quality metrics that feed the feedback loop, so degradation is detected against targets in real time instead of surfacing only when users complain.

task_statement: 1C2 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
question_text: A research orchestrator delegates 'summarize the retrieved sources' to a subagent, but the subagent returns a summary missing the key sources because it never saw them. The orchestrator held the sources in its own context. What is the root cause?

options.text: The subagent's model was too small to summarize the sources
Required context was not passed in the handoff to the subagent
The orchestrator should have used prompt caching for the sources
Retrieval failed, so the sources never existed in any context

explanation: Domain: Solution Design & Architecture | Subdomain: 1C2 Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving | Key Concept: unshared context by default. Subagents do not inherit the orchestrator's context; whatever a subagent needs must be passed explicitly in the handoff. Forgetting this is a primary cause of multi-agent failures, here a summary missing sources the subagent never received.
